title: The Wrestler
full_review:
"The Wrestler" (Fox Searchlight) is a seamy but powerful character portrait set in a landscape of trailer parks and strip malls. A superb Mickey Rourke plays aging professional grappler Randy "the Ram" Robinson. With his quarter-hour of fame two decades behind him, Randy continues to climb into the ring and torture his body until he's felled by a heart attack.

Isolated from the fans, who provided his only emotional support, Randy initiates a tentative romance with Cassidy (Marisa Tomei), a dancer at a local strip club who's seen better days herself. He also makes fumbling efforts to reconnect with his estranged daughter, Stephanie (Evan Rachel Wood).

Director Darren Aronofsky's study of loneliness is unsparing in its portrayal of the titular sport and of the sadistic impulses of those who flock to it. Cassidy quotes verses from Isaiah that refer to the "suffering servant" whose wounds heal others, and compares Randy's ordeals to the torments endured by Jesus (as she saw them played out in Mel Gibson's "The Passion of the Christ").

But there's no tone of irreverence in her comparison.

Despite a high level of violence (sometimes bloody) -- Randy's opponents use props such as barbed wire and a staple gun -- and despite the frank and demeaning sexuality of Cassidy's environment, this drama's artistic intent and achievement are clear.

So too are the fundamentally decent aspirations of the troubled man at its core. Randy's climactic silent prayer, accompanied by tears and ending in the sign of the cross, sees Rourke convey genuine, if desperate, faith with the same assured heft he brings to every moment of this memorable comeback role.

The film contains strong sexual content, including graphic nonmarital sexual activity, some nudity, brutal wrestling scenes, drug abuse, pervasive rough and much crude language, and some profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted. Under 17 requires accompanying parent or adult guardian.
